item.title: Flight to safety concerns from continued cyber issues send stocks lower, yields lower, gold higher, JPY and CHF up
item.description:
Reports that the National Security Agency’s internal communications network is down have added uncertainty to trading. Reuters, citing CNN, reports that the scope is being investigated, with no immediate evidence of a cyberattack. reuters.com

There are also reports circulating about possible Gmail and Microsoft Outlook disruptions, although a fresh widespread outage has not been confirmed. Google’s status dashboard currently lists no incidents. google.com

The market reaction has been a move toward safety. Stocks have moved lower, gold has pushed higher, Treasury yields have backed away from their highs, and buyers have moved into the CHF and JPY.

But have the technicals done enough to confirm that shift?

Nasdaq breaks below its 50% midpoint

The NASDAQ composite has fallen below 24,206.50, the 50% midpoint of the move higher from the end-of-March low to the October high.

That gives sellers another technical break to build on. Staying below the midpoint keeps the sellers more in control. Moving back above would take some of the pressure off and raise the risk of a failed break.

For now, that level becomes a close barometer for buyers and sellers.

Gold moves higher but still faces resistance

Gold extended to a session high of $3,891.07, but remains below its falling 100 hour moving average at $3,906.46.

The flight-to-safety buying has helped. However, if the price is going higher, buyers need to get and stay above that moving average.

Until that happens, sellers still have a level to lean against. A sustained break above would give buyers more control and strengthen the technical case for a further recovery.

Treasury yields retreat, but support remains intact

The US 10 year yield moved from a high near 5.158% to a low of 5.093% as Treasury buying picked up.

However, the yield remains above its rising 100 hour moving average at 5.087%. That is the first downside hurdle. Below that, the swing area between 5.00% and 5.03% becomes the next key target.

Those levels need to be broken to take more of the upside pressure off yields. The retreat is a step lower, but the technical picture has more work to do.

Inflation concerns also remain part of the backdrop following the import and export price data released earlier today.

CHF and JPY attract haven demand

The CHF and JPY have attracted buying against the USD over the last hour of trading as traders move toward traditional safe-haven currencies.

In the video above, I take a look at the technicals across these markets and explain the bias, the risks and the targets given the price action.

The trading lesson: Headlines create the move. Technicals define the risk.

A headline can change sentiment quickly. The technical levels help traders judge whether that initial reaction is gaining traction.

For the NASDAQ, the question is whether sellers can keep the price below its 50% midpoint. For gold, buyers need to clear the 100 hour moving average. For the 10 year yield, a break below its own 100 hour moving average would strengthen the move lower.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Jensen Huang says open to return as CEO if board allows
item.description:
Shares of Nvidia are bouncing after founder Jensen Huang broke his silence. In a statement, he said he was open to returning as CEO if the board allows it.

That news has helped the entire market.

Yesterday, there was a report that the board wasn't even talking about bringing him back but also that employees were considering a protest to bring him back.

The statement says:

"I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely. Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO."

Yesterday, Trump seemed to indicate that he was open to Huang returning, despite all evidence pointing to his own White House as a big part of the smear designed to remove him -- likely the State Dept.

“I would certainly not mind seeing that,” Trump said when asked about Huang returning.

Now we just need employees to tweet "Nvidia is nothing without its people" and Larry Summers to get on the board.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: It's getting tough to believe all these internet outages are a coincidence
item.description:
At some point, coinsidences become a pattern and we're now well-beyond that.

CNN reports that the American National Security Agency's classified internal comms network—NSANet -- is down. It's a highly-classified nework for official use.

This comes on the heels of the Microsoft Office outage, the FAA outage and the outages at banks yesterday. 

Officials keep saying that "there is no evidence of a cyberattack" but that's starting to sound rich. The market is noticing too and there was selling on this headline and yesterday's banking outage. The market is on edge about AI-led attacks, in light of all the warnings from tech executives.

With the downdraft in stocks, the S&P 500 has cut through the 200-day moving average to the lowest since June. Chip stocks are getting hit hard again with Nvidia and Micron among the laggards.

For this NSA outage, I also tend to wonder who is leaking this and if they have a motive for highlighting it. That's normally the kind of thing that would be kept under wraps, not sent to CNN.

In addition, Charles Schwab’s website is reprotedly down for some users, showing an “Internal Server Error” page. The error page points to Akamai, the content delivery network many banks and brokers rely on, which suggests the problem may sit with Akamai rather than Schwab itself. Akamai reported availability problems with its Application Load Balancer on Monday and said it was deploying a fix.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nasdaq stretching toward the swing area and 50% retracement targets. Key support being tested.
item.description:
The Nasdaq Composite has moved sharply lower after breaking below its rising trend channel and key moving averages. Those breaks shifted the technical bias in favor of the sellers. The question now is whether buyers can build a floor against a key support area.

The latest move lower reached 24,427.83. That put the index just above a support zone between the 50% midpoint of the rally from the April low at 24,206.50 and a swing level at 24,425.34.

Buyers leaned against that area and pushed the price higher. That is a start. However, holding support is only part of the battle. To take back control, buyers need to get above—and stay above—the technical levels overhead.

The first hurdles come at:

  • 25,036.33: The 38.2% retracement of the move up from the April low.
  • 25,147.03: The 200 day moving average.
  • 25,329.71: The falling 100 hour moving average.

Those levels create a series of steps the buyers need to climb. Moving above the 38.2% retracement would be encouraging, but getting back above the 200 day moving average and the falling 100 hour moving average would give buyers more technical credibility.

Until then, a rebound remains a correction within a market controlled by the sellers.

Above the 100 hour moving average, the next targets include 25,831.74, followed by the 200 hour moving average near 25,998.65 and the 100 day moving average at 26,153.01.

Conversely, if the price stalls below the overhead resistance and rotates lower, the focus returns to 24,437.83 and the 24,206.50–24,425.34 support area. A break below that zone would open the door toward the 61.8% retracement at 23,376.66.

For traders, the distinction is important. Buyers have a support area to lean against and define risk. But a bounce off support does not automatically change the bias. The buyers need to prove they can reclaim the broken technical levels.

Hold support, and they have a chance. Reclaim resistance, and they start to take back control.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: US Sept business inventories +0.5% vs +0.4% prior
item.description:
• Prior was +0.4%
  • Retail inventories ex-autos +0.5% vs +0.4% prior

This report is rarely a market mover but it's an input into GDP, so a strong number will boost tracking estimates and vice versa.

For background, the Census Bureau’s Manufacturing and Trade Inventories and Sales report, known as business inventories, is released monthly at 10 am ET about six weeks after the reference month ends. It combines inventories and sales across the three main stages of the goods supply chain: manufacturers, wholesalers and retailers.

Much of the report is known by the time it’s released. Manufacturing inventories come out in the factory orders report, and advance estimates for wholesale and retail inventories are published about two weeks earlier in the Advance Economic Indicators release. Business inventories adds the full retail figures and pulls everything into a combined total, so the headline change in total business inventories rarely surprises.

Retail inventories are the most useful piece. They’re broken down by type of store, including motor vehicle and parts dealers, general merchandise, food and beverage stores, clothing, furniture and building materials. Auto dealer inventories swing sharply with production schedules, supply disruptions and incentives, so economists focus on retail inventories excluding autos. That measure feeds directly into the inventory investment component of GDP and often prompts revisions to growth estimates.

The report also includes inventory-to-sales ratios for each sector and in total. A rising ratio can mean demand is softening and stock is piling up, or that businesses are deliberately building buffers. A falling ratio points to lean shelves and the potential for restocking, which can support future production. The figures are in nominal dollars, so higher prices can lift inventory values without any change in physical stock.

Inventories have become a bigger swing factor in recent years. Tariff-driven stockpiling followed by drawdowns has created large distortions in quarterly GDP, making the retail detail more relevant than usual.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Home Depot earnings offer a mixed picture of the US consumer as spending improves but traffic remains weak
item.description:
Home Depot reported better-than-expected third-quarter earnings and sales on Tuesday but shares fell 1.9% in premarket trading as the company faces margin pressure. It's the first of the major retailers to report this week.

The home improvement giant reported adjusted earnings of $3.86 per share compared to $3.84 expected, while revenue of $43.4 billion topped the $42.8 billion consensus.

The more interesting numbers are buried deeper in the report and offer some clues about the health of the US consumer.

Comparable sales rose 2.2% in the quarter, including a matching 2.2% increase in the US. That's an improvement from the 0.2% growth reported a year ago and suggests some stabilization in home improvement spending.

However, the composition of that growth is telling.

  • Comparable sales: +2.2%

  • Comparable customer transactions: -0.5%

  • Comparable average ticket: +3.0%

  • Average ticket: $93.09 versus $90.39 a year ago

In other words, customers are spending more when they visit Home Depot, but they're still visiting and buying less frequently. It looks more like inflation than a healthy consumer but there is some sequential improvement here. Transactions fell 1.6% in the same quarter last year, so the pace of decline has moderated considerably. Still, the recovery in spending is being driven by larger tickets rather than more transactions.

The company doesn't break down how much of the increase in average ticket comes from inflation, larger projects or customers purchasing more expensive products. That makes it difficult to draw conclusions about real consumption.

Another complication is Home Depot's growing professional contractor business, including its acquisitions of SRS Distribution and GMS. That business is increasingly important to total revenues but doesn't necessarily reflect the spending decisions of ordinary households.

Home Depot has been fighting a difficult housing market and is particularly exposed to interest rates. Elevated mortgage costs have kept homeowners locked into existing properties and depressed housing turnover, which is a major lever renovation and improvement spending.

On guidance, Home Depot now expects full-year comparable sales growth of 1.4% and adjusted earnings growth of approximately 2%. The earnings forecast implies adjusted EPS of roughly $14.98, slightly below the $15.05 analysts had expected.

The company also lowered its operating margin outlook to the bottom of its previous range, despite moving its total sales growth forecast to the top of the prior range.

That's a disappointing combination. Revenue rose 4.9% in the quarter but operating income increased just 2.4%, suggesting that stronger sales aren't translating into much additional profitability. I wonder if they start to pull on the price-hike lever, adding to consumer inflation.

For the US economic outlook, I would characterize the report as mildly encouraging but far from a signal that the consumer is roaring. Today's US retail sales report was also solid.

The slowdown in transaction declines is a positive sign and argues against a sharp deterioration in household spending. At the same time, the continued decline in traffic suggests consumers remain selective, particularly when it comes to expensive discretionary home improvement projects.

For now, though, the message is that the US consumer is holding up, but there is still considerable reluctance to spend. There might be more color in the call so I'll look out for details.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: NAHB housing market index for November 25 vs 29 estimate
item.description:
• Prior 29

Builder confidence weakens across all components, with current sales posting the largest decline.

  • The NAHB/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index fell 4 points to 25 in November from 29 in October. That is the lowest reading over the past year and compares with 38 in November 2025.

The index remains well below the 50 level that separates positive from negative builder sentiment. The weakness is also broadening, with current sales, expectations for future sales and buyer traffic all moving lower.

The components showed:

  • Current single-family sales fell 6 points to 28 from 34.
  • Sales expectations for the next six months fell 2 points to 30 from 32.
  • Traffic of prospective buyers fell 2 points to 16 from 18.

The sharpest deterioration came in current sales. That component has fallen 11 points since August, suggesting builders are seeing conditions weaken as the year progresses.

Buyer traffic at 16 is another concern. Expectations for future sales are holding above assessments of current sales, but at 30, builders are hardly signaling confidence in a meaningful turnaround.

The regional data also showed declines across all four regions in November:

  • Northeast fell 6 points to 31.
  • Midwest fell 5 points to 30.
  • South fell 5 points to 23.
  • West fell 1 point to 19.

The three-month moving averages, which smooth out monthly volatility, reinforced the weaker trend. The Northeast fell to 34 from 38, the Midwest to 35 from 40, the South to 27 from 30 and the West to 23 from 26.

For the housing market, there is little encouragement in this report. Current sales are weakening, buyer traffic remains depressed, and expectations continue to move lower. Buyers need to show up before builders can become more confident. November’s numbers suggest that improvement remains elusive.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bitcoin is continuing the consolidation but sellers remain in control
item.description:
Sellers have controlled the technical breaks.

Going back to November 5, Bitcoin fell below its 100 and 200 hour moving averages and its 100 day moving average—all on the same day. That series of breaks shifted control firmly toward the sellers.

The sellers then leaned against the falling 100 hour moving average on November 9 and again on November 11. Buyers could not get above that moving average, and the subsequent break below the 200 day moving average—currently at $72,799—gave sellers another go-ahead to push lower.

They did.

The decline finally reached a low of $61,947 on Sunday. The price rebounded to $66,069 later that day before settling into a consolidation, with support developing near $63,815.

The 100 hour moving average is catching up.

The consolidation over the last two or so days has allowed the falling 100 hour moving average to catch up with the price. That moving average currently comes in at $65,654.

Today’s high reached $65,123, leaving the price $531 short of that technical barometer. However, with the moving average continuing to fall, decision time is getting closer for both buyers and sellers.

In the video, I outline why that moving average matters and the levels that would either keep sellers in control or give buyers an opportunity for a larger corrective move.

Stay below, and sellers keep the advantage.

As long as the price remains below the 100 hour moving average, sellers retain control. Buyers have stabilized the price after the sharp decline, but they still need to show they can take back a technical level.

On the downside, the levels to watch are:

  • $63,815: The consolidation floor. A break below would open the door for renewed selling.
  • $61,947: Sunday’s low and the next downside target if that floor gives way.

Holding support can slow a decline. Getting above resistance is what starts to change the bias.

What would give buyers more hope?

A move above the 100 hour moving average at $65,654—and the ability to stay above it—would give buyers their first meaningful technical improvement.

That would put the next upside targets in play:

  • $66,069: Sunday’s corrective high.
  • $69,265: The 38.2% retracement of the decline from the November high.
  • $69,460: The falling 200 hour moving average.

The retracement and 200 hour moving average form a higher resistance area. However, buyers first need to get through the 100 hour moving average and Sunday’s corrective high before that area becomes a more immediate focus.

The education: Consolidation gives the moving averages time to catch up.

After a sharp trend move, a market can correct through price, through time, or through a combination of both.

Bitcoin’s recent sideways trading is allowing the falling 100 hour moving average to move closer to the market. That creates a clearer decision point without requiring a large rally.

For sellers, the moving average becomes a level to lean against and define risk. Stay below, and the bearish bias remains intact. Move above and hold above, and some of that control starts to shift toward the buyers.

For buyers, a bounce from the low is a start. Breaking and holding above a moving average that has repeatedly capped rallies is stronger evidence of progress.

For now, the sellers remain in control. The 100 hour moving average is the barometer for a change.

Be aware. Be prepared.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: US October industrial production -0.4% vs +0.1% expected
item.description:
• Prior was +0.7%
  • Capacity utilization 76.4% vs 76.8% exp
  • Manufacturing output +0.3% vs +0.2% expected
  • Prior manufacturing output +0.3%
  • Mining -0.8% vs +0.2% prior
  • Utilities -4.3% vs +3.5% prior
  • Y/y +2.1% vs +2.25% prior

Utilities caused the miss. They gave back September’s weather-driven 4.4% jump: electric output fell 4.2% and natural gas utilities fell 4.7%. The utility operating rate fell 3.3 points to 70.2%. Even so, electric output is still up 2.0% y/y.

Deeper into the report, there are good signs. Motor vehicles and parts rose 4.4% after falling 2.7% in September. Semiconductor output rose 2.2% m/m and is up 15.3% y/y (though that's likely driven by pricing, not volumes). Business equipment was up 1.0%, and +7.8% y/y so that's a good sign on future productivity.

The annual revision is due November 24 and will rebase the index to 2022, so expect these numbers to be redrawn next week.

For background, the Federal Reserve’s industrial production report, formally the G.17 release on Industrial Production and Capacity Utilization, is published monthly at 9:15 am ET, usually around the middle of the month. It measures the real output of the US industrial sector and is one of the few major economic reports produced by the Fed itself.

The headline industrial production index covers three sectors: manufacturing, which accounts for roughly three-quarters of the total, mining and utilities. Mining includes oil and gas extraction and drilling, so it tracks swings in energy prices and rig activity. Utilities output is driven largely by weather, with hot summers and cold winters pushing electricity and gas demand higher. Because both can swing the headline, markets often focus on manufacturing output as the cleaner read on factory activity. Within manufacturing, motor vehicles and parts are the most volatile category, sensitive to plant shutdowns, retooling and strikes.

The report also includes capacity utilization, the share of available industrial capacity in use. It’s watched as a gauge of slack in the economy. High utilization has historically been associated with rising inflation pressure and stronger business investment, as firms run close to their limits. Low utilization suggests idle capacity and weak demand. Readings are often compared with the long-run average, around the high 70s.

Unlike the regional Fed surveys and PMIs, industrial production measures actual physical output rather than sentiment, though it’s subject to revision as more complete data arrive.

The report rarely moves markets significantly, but it’s an important input for tracking GDP and the business cycle. Recent attention has focused on reshoring, tariffs and investment in high-tech equipment and data center power.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: US October advance retail sales +0.2% vs +0.2% expected
item.description:
• Prior was +0.8%
  • Ex autos +0.6% vs +0.4% expected
  • Prior ex-autos +0.9% (revised to +1.1%)
  • Retail sales control group +0.6% vs +0.4% expected
  • Prior control was +0.1% (revised to +0.5%)
  • Ex autos and gas +0.5% vs +0.2% prior
  • Retail sales y/y nominal +6.82% vs +6.29% prior

Details:

  • Gasoline +1.5% m/m vs +6.4% m/m prior
  • Nonstore retailers +1.2% m/m vs +0.3% m/m prior
  • Electronics and appliances 0.0% m/m vs +0.6% m/m prior
  • Sporting goods and hobbies -0.7% m/m vs -0.5% m/m prior
  • Restaurants and bars +0.2% m/m vs +1.1% m/m prior
  • Building materials +0.5% vs -0.6% prior
  • Furniture -2.3% vs +1.3% prior

    Ahead of the report, the market was pricing in 61 bps in hikes through March and that's ticked up to 63 bps but some of that could be from the import/export price data released at the same time, which was hot. The US dollar is broadly stronger in the aftermath by around a dozen pips.

    In terms of this report, there are some real positives around the consumer, once again. The revisions higher from the prior were meaningful and the key readings still beat. You would like to see better numbers on furniture and appliances but it's not shocking that they missed, given the slump in housing. 

    A short time ago, Home Depot reported better earnings that expected, which is a good sign for hte consumer. However shares are down 1.9% on a slightly softer guide on 2027 EPS, (though it was slightly better on revenue, so this could be a margin story). The CEO was also replaced due to health issues so that could be a factor as well. 

    For background, the US Census Bureau’s advance retail sales report is the earliest comprehensive read on consumer spending each month. It’s released at 8:30 am ET, usually around the middle of the month, just two weeks after the reference month ends, which makes it one of the most timely and market-moving US data releases.

    The headline is the seasonally adjusted monthly change in total retail and food services sales. The report covers 13 major categories, including motor vehicles and parts, gasoline stations, grocery stores, general merchandise, building materials, health and personal care, clothing, electronics, furniture and nonstore retailers, the category that captures online shopping. Food services and drinking places, covering restaurants and bars, is the only services category, and it’s watched as a gauge of discretionary spending.

    Because auto sales and gasoline prices swing the headline, markets focus on several narrower measures. Sales excluding autos and sales excluding autos and gas strip out the most volatile pieces. The control group, which also excludes building materials and food services, is the most important for economists, because it feeds directly into the goods portion of personal consumption expenditures in GDP. A strong or weak control group often prompts immediate revisions to growth forecasts.

    The figures are in nominal dollars and aren’t adjusted for inflation, so rising prices can inflate sales without any increase in volumes. Comparing them with goods inflation in CPI gives a sense of real spending. The advance estimate is based on a smaller sample and is revised in each of the following two months, sometimes enough to change the narrative.

    Retail sales also capture shifts in behavior, such as consumers pulling purchases forward ahead of tariffs or cutting back when prices rise.

    This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: US Import prices 1.1% vs 0.7% est. Export prices 1.1% vs 0.5% est.
item.description:
US October import prices rise 1.1% as nonfuel inflation accelerates

  • Import prices MoM: +1.1%. Prior +1.1%. YoY 8.1%

  • Export prices MoM: +1.1%. Prior revised to +2.4% vs 2.2% originally reported.  YoY 11.8%

  • Nonfuel import prices MoM: +0.8%. Prior revised to +0.5%

October components compared with September:

  • Fuel import prices: +3.6% vs +6.3%.
  • Nonfuel industrial supplies import prices: +0.5% vs +0.2%.
  • Food, feed and beverage import prices: −0.2% vs +0.4%.
  • Agricultural export prices: +1.2% vs +2.7%.
  • Nonagricultural export prices: +1.1% vs +2.4%.

US import prices rose 1.1% in October, matching September’s increase, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The inflation signal remained firm as nonfuel import prices accelerated even as fuel-price gains slowed. Export prices also increased 1.1%, easing from September’s revised 2.4% advance. 2026 M10 Results

The standout was imported capital goods, where prices jumped 1.5%—the largest monthly increase since the series began in December 1988. Computers, peripherals, semiconductors and machinery helped drive the gain. Prices for imports from China rose 1.4%, the largest monthly increase since that series began in January 2004.

Headline year-over-year comparisons are unavailable because the 2025 government shutdown prevented collection of some October 2025 data.

Quick analysis: The concern for the Fed is the broadening pressure beyond energy. Higher equipment and consumer-goods import prices could feed into business costs and retail prices, although the pass-through is uncertain. That normally supports a firmer dollar and higher Treasury yields as traders reassess the inflation outlook. Slower fuel-price gains and falling food import prices provide some offset.

What this report measures: The Import and Export Price Indexes track changes in prices for goods and selected services traded between the United States and other countries. Import prices exclude tariffs, so this is not a direct measure of tariff costs. Traders monitor the monthly figures for signs of inflation pressure moving through international trade; recent readings are subject to revision.

Digging Deeper at Imported Inflation

The biggest issue is that imported inflation is spreading beyond energy. Fuel prices are lifting the headline, but capital goods—and machinery in particular—are creating a broader pipeline of price pressure.

  • Capital goods are the biggest concern. They represent 31.2% of imports, and prices rose 1.5% in October after increases of 1.1%, 0.9%, and 1.0% in the preceding three months. That is persistent pressure on the equipment businesses buy, with the monthly increase accelerating.

  • Machinery is the main driver within capital goods. Nonelectrical machinery accounts for nearly 25% of imports. Prices rose 1.7% in October after three consecutive increases of 1.2%. That puts the cumulative four-month increase near 5.4%. This is a large category showing sustained increases.

  • Energy is adding another significant push. Fuel prices rose 3.6% after September’s 6.3% increase. Petroleum rose 3.7% in October and is up 46.8% from a year earlier. Natural gas increased 5.1% for the month, although its small weight limits its overall impact.

  • The underlying measures are moving in the wrong direction. Import prices excluding food and fuels rose 0.9%, up from 0.5% in September. Prices excluding fuels increased 0.8%. Those numbers make it difficult to dismiss the report as simply an energy story.

  • Consumer goods and autos show smaller but continuing increases. Consumer goods rose 0.5%, with durable goods up 0.6%. Automotive imports increased 0.4%. Together, those categories account for roughly 38% of imports, so even moderate increases matter.

  • Food and unfinished metals provided some relief. Food prices fell 0.2%, while unfinished metals declined 1.0%. However, finished metals rose 2.1% and nonmetal materials for durable goods increased 2.0%.

Using the reported weights as a rough guide, capital goods contributed about 0.47 percentage point to October’s increase, versus approximately 0.34 point from fuels. Those estimates show why machinery deserves at least as much attention as oil.

For the inflation outlook, the concern is the combination: higher energy costs alongside persistent increases in business equipment and firmer consumer goods prices. That creates pressure at several points in the supply chain, although the eventual pass-through to consumers is not automatic.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

U.S. import and export prices both increased by 1.1% in October, with continued upward pressure on prices across international trade. Import prices matched September’s 1.1% increase, while export prices slowed from a stronger 2.4% advance in the previous month.

The rise in import prices was driven by higher costs for both fuel and nonfuel goods. Nonfuel import prices also gathered pace, increasing 0.8% after rising 0.5% in September. Higher prices for capital goods, consumer goods excluding automotives, nonfuel industrial supplies and materials, and automotive products more than offset lower food, feed and beverage prices.

On the export side, prices advanced 1.1% in October, with gains across both agricultural and nonagricultural goods. Nonagricultural export prices also increased 1.1%, following a 2.4% advance in September. Higher prices for industrial supplies and materials, consumer goods excluding automotives, and automotive products supported the monthly rise. 

Due to the 2025 federal government shutdown and a lapse in appropriations, the agency did not collect survey data for October 2025. As a result, it could not publish October 2025 indexes for series that primarily rely on survey data, meaning the y/y price changes for October 2026 are unavailable.

item.title: Riddle: Buyers were more aggressive, yet stock prices fell. How is that possible?
item.description:
When financial commentators say buyers were more aggressive than sellers, what exactly do they mean?

And if every trade has a buyer and a seller, how can there be more buying than selling? Let's solve a market riddle that explains how trading really works.

Imagine reading a financial article that says:

"Buyers were more aggressive than sellers, yet prices continued to fall."

Wait a minute. Doesn't that sound contradictory?

If buyers are more aggressive, shouldn't prices go up?

And what does "aggressive buying" even mean? Are people buying more shares? Are wealthy investors spending more money? Are there more buyers than sellers?

The answer is surprisingly interesting, and understanding it can change how you think about financial markets.

You don't need to be a professional trader, understand complicated charts or even own a single share to follow along.

Let's start with the basics.

First, what does it mean to be an aggressive buyer?

Imagine you want to buy one share of a company.

You check its price and discover something interesting.

There isn't really just one price. There are two prices that matter when you're about to trade.

$99.95 is the bid. That's the highest price someone is currently offering to pay for a share.

$100.00 is the ask. That's the lowest price someone is currently offering to accept for a share.

The difference between those prices, five cents, is called the spread.

Now you have two choices.

Choice 1: You're a patient buyer

You decide you don't want to pay $100.

Instead, you place an order saying:

"I'll buy one share, but only for $99.95 or less."

This is called a limit buy order.

Your order can wait until someone is willing to sell at that price.

Maybe someone accepts your offer in a few seconds. Maybe it takes an hour. Perhaps nobody accepts it.

You are behaving as a passive buyer.

You're offering to buy at your chosen price and waiting for someone else to come to you.

Choice 2: You're an aggressive buyer

This time, you don't want to wait.

You see someone offering to sell at $100, and you decide to accept that price immediately.

You place a market buy order.

Assuming the share is still available, your purchase executes at $100.

Congratulations! You've just become an aggressive buyer.

But here's something important.

Being aggressive doesn't necessarily mean you're extremely bullish, rich, impatient by nature or making a risky decision.

It simply describes how you executed your trade.

An aggressive buyer accepts an available selling price rather than waiting for a seller to accept their buying price.

And sellers can behave aggressively too.

A seller who wants to sell immediately can accept the best available buying price, rather than waiting for someone to pay more.

In market terminology, traders who execute against available orders are taking liquidity. Traders whose orders wait to be executed are providing liquidity.

One small detail: A limit order can also be aggressive if its price allows it to execute immediately. What matters is whether the order takes available liquidity or waits to provide it.

Now we understand what aggressive buying means.

But that creates another interesting question.

How can there be more buying than selling if every trade needs both?

Here's one of the most important facts about the stock market:

For every share that somebody buys, somebody else must sell that same share.

Always.

Imagine 1,000 shares of a company change hands.

That means exactly 1,000 shares were bought and exactly 1,000 shares were sold.

You cannot have 1,200 shares bought and only 800 sold in completed transactions.

Think of it like buying a bicycle from someone. You can't purchase the bicycle unless someone sells it to you.

Financial markets work on the same basic principle.

Now, an important distinction: The number of people buying and selling doesn't have to be equal.

One investor could sell 1,000 shares to ten different people buying 100 shares each.

That's one seller and ten buyers, but still exactly 1,000 shares bought and 1,000 shares sold.

So whenever you hear someone saying "there was more buying than selling," remember that they cannot literally mean more shares were bought than sold.

They usually mean something different.

And that brings us to a fascinating indicator called Volume Delta.

What is Volume Delta, and what does positive Delta mean?

Don't let the name intimidate you.

Volume simply refers to how many shares or contracts were traded.

Delta measures the difference between the volume of trades initiated by aggressive buyers and the volume initiated by aggressive sellers.

Let's make it incredibly simple.

Imagine that during five minutes of trading, 10,000 shares change hands.

Of those transactions:

  • 7,000 shares were traded because aggressive buyers accepted the available selling prices.

  • 3,000 shares were traded because aggressive sellers accepted the available buying prices.

The calculation is:

7,000 - 3,000 = +4,000

That's called positive Volume Delta.

It tells us that more of the traded volume was initiated by buyers than by sellers.

But remember our earlier lesson!

There were still exactly 10,000 shares bought and 10,000 shares sold.

The difference is who initiated the transactions, not how many shares were bought versus sold.

Here's another way to understand it.

When an aggressive buyer purchases 100 shares from a passive seller, those 100 shares count toward aggressive buying volume.

They don't also count as 100 shares of aggressive selling, because the seller was the one waiting with an offer.

Likewise, if an aggressive seller sells 100 shares to a passive buyer, those shares count toward aggressive selling volume.

Every transaction has two sides, but Delta identifies which side initiated the trade.

Positive Delta means buyer-initiated volume was greater. Negative Delta means seller-initiated volume was greater.

Some trading platforms can estimate this distinction from the prices at which transactions occur relative to available bids and offers. That's why a specialist trading indicator can provide information that isn't obvious from an ordinary price chart.

And you don't need to use such an indicator yourself to understand what a market commentator is describing.

Now for our riddle: What happens when aggressive buyers meet patient sellers?

Imagine a stock trading at $100.

Lots of people want to buy it immediately.

They keep accepting offers to purchase shares at $100.

Surely the price must rise?

Not necessarily.

Imagine a large investment fund wants to sell 100,000 shares.

The fund doesn't necessarily want to dump all those shares onto the market immediately. Instead, it might place limit sell orders and wait for buyers.

Here's what could happen.

Aggressive buyers purchase 5,000 shares at $100.

But more shares become available for sale at $100.

Buyers purchase another 10,000 shares.

More selling offers appear.

The buying continues, yet the stock struggles to rise above $100.

What's happening?

Buyers are aggressively purchasing shares, but sellers are supplying enough shares to satisfy that demand without requiring higher prices.

One side is eager to buy. The other is prepared to sell, but doesn't need to chase the buyers.

This is an important lesson.

A large amount of aggressive buying does not automatically produce a large price increase.

Sometimes patient sellers can meet that demand for an extended period.

Traders sometimes call this behavior absorption, because available selling liquidity is absorbing the aggressive buying.

However, we cannot automatically identify those sellers as institutions. There might be one large participant, many smaller sellers, market makers or a combination of them.

And a positive Delta reading by itself doesn't prove that absorption occurred.

But how can the price actually FALL with positive Delta?

Let's take our example one step further.

Imagine that the stock begins trading around $100.

During a short period, aggressive buyers purchase 700 shares at $100.

There are enough sellers offering shares at that price, so those purchases don't push the stock higher.

Then conditions change.

Some buying orders disappear from the market, and aggressive sellers begin accepting lower available bids.

Another 300 shares trade as sellers accept those bids, with the final transactions occurring at $99.80.

Let's look at what happened.

Look at that!

Delta was positive, but the stock price fell.

Remember, the total number of shares bought and sold was equal: 1,000 on each side.

Why did the price fall?

Because the aggressive buying was matched by enough selling supply at $100, while subsequent selling moved transactions to lower available prices.

Price movement depends not only on the total amount of aggressive buying and selling but also on when the transactions take place and how much liquidity is available at different prices.

In other words, buying and selling pressure don't always move prices with equal effectiveness.

This is why professional traders sometimes compare buying effort with actual price progress.

It's one thing for buyers to be aggressive.

It's another thing for them to succeed in pushing prices higher.

Why do large institutions often prefer patient orders?

Let's imagine you want to buy five shares of a company.

Your order is relatively small, so executing it immediately might have little effect on the market price of a liquid stock.

Now imagine managing a large pension fund that wants to buy one million shares.

That creates a different problem.

If the fund tries to purchase all one million shares immediately, it might exhaust the shares available at the lowest asking price.

To complete its purchase, it may have to accept increasingly expensive offers.

The fund could end up paying substantially more than it originally expected.

That's called market impact.

To manage this problem, institutions often use limit orders and execution algorithms that split large transactions into smaller orders.

They might spread their buying or selling over minutes, hours or even days, depending on their objectives and market conditions.

The goal is often to reduce unnecessary price impact and transaction costs.

Of course, waiting carries risks too.

A large buyer who insists on a particular price might never get all the shares they want. And if the market rises while they're waiting, the eventual purchase could become more expensive.

This is why sophisticated participants use a combination of aggressive and passive execution.

Institutions don't always trade passively, and individual investors don't always trade aggressively.

But understanding why large investors may prefer patient execution helps explain something that otherwise seems strange:

A very large seller can participate in substantial trading activity without necessarily appearing as aggressive selling volume.

The seller may simply be waiting for aggressive buyers to trade against their offers.

An example from S&P 500 futures

This isn't merely a hypothetical lesson.

On November 16, 2026, E-mini S&P 500 futures, a widely traded contract linked to the S&P 500 index, provided an interesting example.

During the session, ES declined 138.75 index points from its opening price to its closing price.

Yet cumulative Volume Delta ended positive by approximately 4,660 contracts.

Cumulative Volume Delta, or CVD, is simply a running total of Volume Delta over a chosen period.

So despite greater buyer-initiated volume across the session, the market suffered a substantial decline.

That doesn't prove who was selling, why they were selling or what would happen next.

But it demonstrates why positive Delta shouldn't automatically be interpreted as a bullish trading signal.

The aggressive buying and the actual price performance were telling different parts of the story.

What can an ordinary investor learn from all this?

You don't need to become a day trader or start using sophisticated order-flow indicators to benefit from understanding this concept.

The lesson applies to anyone who follows financial markets.

When you hear that there's "strong buying," it's worth asking what that actually means.

Is the price rising? Is it holding those gains? Is the buying really producing meaningful progress?

And when someone says there are "more buyers than sellers," remember that every completed transaction involves equal quantities bought and sold.

The distinction is often about which side is more eager to execute and which side is prepared to wait.

Even if you've never used Volume Delta, understanding this difference can help you interpret market commentary more intelligently.

The answer to our riddle

How can aggressive buying exceed aggressive selling while prices decline?

Because aggressive buying measures who is taking the initiative to trade, not who is ultimately succeeding in moving prices in their preferred direction.

Buyers can repeatedly accept available offers without moving prices higher if enough selling liquidity is available.

And if the market subsequently finds willing sellers at lower prices, the price can decline despite positive Delta over the measured period.

That's why one of the most useful lessons from order flow is also one of the simplest:

Aggression measures the effort. Price movement shows the result.

And in financial markets, understanding the difference can be more valuable than simply knowing who appears to be buying or selling more aggressively.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.description:
S&P 500 futures: Why a move above 7,425 may not be enough for bulls ahead of Nvidia earnings

ES futures face several closely packed technical obstacles as traders prepare for Nvidia's earnings. The bearish outlook remains intact for now, but buyers have a potential path to recovery if they can do more than briefly push prices above resistance.

S&P 500 E-mini futures (ES) were trading around 7,412 during my analysis on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. My directional preference remains bearish, although I am watching for evidence that buyers are regaining control. The first important challenge is around 7,425, but a move above that level alone would not persuade me that the market has turned bullish.

This is a conditional tradeCompass outlook, not a prediction about where futures must trade next.

Why 7,425 could be a difficult hurdle for buyers

What makes the area around 7,425 particularly interesting is that several market references are concentrated within a relatively narrow price range.

At the time of the analysis, the following levels were relevant:

  • Around 7,415: The lower first standard-deviation band of today's developing volume-weighted average price (VWAP).

  • 7,423.50: Today's developing value-area low.

  • 7,424.25: Yesterday's value-area low.

  • Around 7,429-7,430: Today's developing VWAP.

  • Around 7,434: Yesterday's point of control, the price with the greatest traded volume in that session's profile.

These levels help explain why a rebound from around 7,400 might run into difficulties before buyers establish a more convincing recovery.

The value area represents a region where a substantial proportion of a session's volume was transacted. Re-entering it can be an encouraging first step for bulls, but it does not automatically mean buyers are back in control.

There is a meaningful difference between trading above a level and being accepted above it.

For example, ES could rally above 7,425, trade briefly around 7,430 or even 7,434, and subsequently reverse lower. In that case, the advance might tell us more about the failure of buyers to maintain progress than about the beginning of a sustainable bullish reversal.

Conversely, if buyers reclaim these prices, defend them during a pullback and continue making progress, the bearish interpretation would become less convincing.

This is why I would not automatically place a limit buy order simply because ES approaches or crosses 7,425 from below.

Buyers have been active. Their price progress tells a different story.

One of the more interesting observations from the recent trading activity is that aggressive buying has not consistently translated into higher prices. How is that even possible? Here is some helpful education about that.

On November 16, ES declined 138.75 points from the session opening price to its closing price, even as cumulative volume delta finished positive by approximately 4,660 contracts.

Cumulative volume delta compares trading volume executed aggressively at the ask with volume executed aggressively at the bid.

A positive reading generally indicates more aggressive buying than selling. However, it does not necessarily indicate that buyers are winning.

In this case, buying aggression was insufficient to sustain higher prices.

That distinction matters because traders sometimes interpret positive order flow as an automatic bullish signal.

The more useful question is whether the buying actually produces price progress that the market can retain.

For ES to demonstrate improving bullish strength, I would want to see buyers holding reclaimed levels rather than repeatedly surrendering advances.

The bearish roadmap: 7,386, 7,371 and 7,360

My preferred scenario remains bearish while ES struggles below the nearby resistance cluster.

If buyers fail to reclaim and retain the 7,423.50-7,434 area, the next downside references I am monitoring are:

7,386: First nearby bearish reference

A move toward this area would suggest the recent rebound has not significantly repaired the weaker market structure.

7,371: Last week's opening price

This is an especially interesting reference because it corresponds to the opening price of the previous CME trading week, beginning Sunday evening, November 8.

As of the research snapshot, the current week's price action had not revisited that opening price.

There is no rule requiring the market to return there. Nevertheless, it provides a meaningful historical reference for assessing whether sellers continue to make progress.

Around 7,360: Another downside reaction area

This region sits close to an earlier historical low around 7,363.75. A sustained move below the preceding levels could bring it back into focus.

Beyond these nearer references, I am also monitoring 7,324 and 7,232 as potential longer-horizon downside areas.

These are considerably more distant possibilities, not forecasts for today's session. A move toward them would require further evidence of bearish continuation.

What would make me reconsider the bearish view?

The most important initial development would be a convincing recovery above the value-area and VWAP cluster around 7,425-7,434.

But 7,445 is my next important bullish threshold.

A sustained move above that level would improve the case that buyers are doing more than producing another temporary rebound.

The subsequent upside areas to inspect would be:

  • 7,481: First higher recovery reference.

  • 7,504: Next potential test of buying strength.

  • 7,522: Additional upside reference.

  • 7,569: A more distant recovery objective if the bullish structure continues improving.

These are sequential areas to evaluate, not promises that ES will visit them and not automatic instructions to buy or sell.

One possible confirmation would be a successful retest of previously reclaimed resistance, showing that buyers are prepared to defend higher prices.

A reversal back beneath the 7,425-7,434 area would weaken that interpretation.

Nvidia earnings could change the outlook, but there are earlier catalysts

Nvidia is scheduled to announce its third-quarter fiscal 2027 financial results at approximately 4:20 p.m. ET on November 17, with its conference call beginning at 5:00 p.m. ET.

The announcement matters beyond Nvidia shareholders.

Nvidia's prominence in semiconductor and artificial intelligence markets means its results and guidance can influence sentiment in the Nasdaq-100 and potentially the broader S&P 500.

A favorable report could encourage buyers to revisit higher technical levels, although a positive earnings result does not guarantee a positive stock-market reaction.

Equally, a disappointing reaction could reinforce existing weakness.

There are also important economic releases before Nvidia reports.

U.S. October retail sales are scheduled for 8:30 a.m. ET, followed by industrial production at 9:15 a.m. ET. Both could affect market expectations and price action during the session.

The implication for traders is straightforward: technical levels help define the conditions to watch, but new information can quickly alter the market's behavior around them.

Sometimes the better trade is no trade

There is a third possibility worth considering.

ES could continue fluctuating between the vicinity of 7,395-7,400 and the resistance region extending toward 7,445, without either buyers or sellers establishing convincing follow-through.

For a trader looking to join a meaningful move, that could be an unattractive environment.

Buying too early risks entering into resistance. Shorting too late can mean entering after much of the immediate decline has already taken place.

The discipline is not simply to correctly identify a directional bias. It is also to recognize when price action offers a sufficiently convincing reason to act.

Futures leverage makes this particularly important. Each index point represents $50 per E-mini S&P 500 futures contract, compared with $5 per Micro E-mini contract. A hypothetical adverse move of 10 points represents $500 or $50 per contract respectively, before trading costs and slippage.

My ES tradeCompass conclusion

My skew for S&P 500 futures remains bearish for now.

Around 7,425, buyers encounter their first important test. Merely crossing that level does not mean they have passed it.

A stronger recovery would involve acceptance through the 7,425-7,434 cluster and ultimately above 7,445.

Until that happens, I am keeping 7,386, last week's opening price at 7,371, and the lower technical references on my watchlist.

Nvidia earnings could substantially alter the picture, in either direction.

The purpose of this tradeCompass is to identify the relevant tests and respond to the evidence, rather than become attached to a forecast.

The hawkish repricing should now be mostly over, as a rate hike in December is widely expected, while the probability of a 50 bps hike remains very slim given that the majority of Fed members favour smaller steps.

It looks like growth concerns are finally gaining traction, with the stock market erasing almost all of last week's gains and Treasury yields slowly rolling over. These concerns are likely to persist and might even intensify as long as the US-Iran situation remains unresolved, and the Fed maintains the hawkish stance.

I think that in the current context, a prolonged US-Iran stalemate or an escalation would keep inflation expectations high alongside a weakening growth outlook, creating a stagflationary environment. And this should ultimately be bullish for gold.

At the same time, if there’s a breakthrough, we could see a dovish repricing on easing inflation concerns, which should also support gold in the short-term.

There are certainly strong headwinds for gold at the moment amid rising real yields and stronger US dollar, so these fundamental views will need to be paired with technicals for a confirmation of a change in momentum.

item.title: Germany November ZEW economic sentiment 35.6 vs 28.8 expected
item.description:
• Prior was 28.1
  • Current conditions -33.2 vs -35.3 expected
  • Prior -35.9
  • Expectations 26.5 vs 18.5 expected
  • Full report

The November ZEW survey showed a significant improvement in German economic sentiment, with expectations rising more than anticipated and pointing to a gradually strengthening recovery.

The headline Economic Sentiment Index increased to 35.6 from 28.1, comfortably beating expectations of 28.8. The Current Conditions Index also improved, rising to -33.2 from -35.9 and beating the -35.3 consensus. Meanwhile, the Expectations Index jumped to 26.5 from 18.5, suggesting that investors and analysts are becoming increasingly optimistic about the economic outlook.

According to ZEW President Achim Wambach, the German economy remains on its recovery path, although the pace of improvement is still subdued. Increasing manufacturing orders and falling oil prices are expected to provide additional support to the recovery.

However, the underlying picture remains uneven across industries. Energy-intensive sectors are showing diverging trends, with the chemical, pharmaceutical and electrical industries reporting significant improvements, while prospects for metal production have deteriorated. The construction sector also remains under pressure, with its index slipping further into negative territory.

Government spending has been the main driver of economic improvement so far, but this has also raised concerns about the long-term sustainability of public debt. This is particularly relevant given Germany's increasing reliance on fiscal expansion to support domestic demand and investment.

Sentiment across the Eurozone also improved, with the Expectations Index rising by 8 points to 26.5. However, the assessment of current economic conditions remained broadly unchanged at -14.7, highlighting the continued gap between improving expectations and still-weak underlying activity.

The data doesn't change anything for the ECB as a rate hike for December is already fully priced in, with traders expecting at least another one next year.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

What are FX option expiries?

The FX option expiration price levels refer to the strike prices where option contracts are set to expire. These levels include both calls and puts.

When you see "EUR/USD at 1.1600 for €4 billion" it means there is a total of €4 billion worth of options (calls + puts combined) that have a strike price of 1.1600 and are expiring at that specific time (the "New York Cut" at 10:00 AM ET).

Traders watch these levels because they often act as a "magnet" for the price. For example, if there's nothing happening in the market and the price is close to the expiry level, let's say 30-50 pips away, what you will usually see is the price moving into the expiry level. This happens due to the hedging activity of the market makers (banks, dealers and so on).

As the price gets closer to the strike price near expiration, these market makers must aggressively buy or sell the currency to hedge their risk. This hedging activity tends to suppress volatility and keep the price "pinned" close to the strike price until the expiration time passes.
